media:group.media:title: What is a spherical tokamak?
media:group.media:description:
To make fusion an efficient and cost-effective energy source, scientists are exploring a compact fusion system design known as a spherical tokamak. Shaped more like a cored apple than the doughnut-like shape of conventional tokamaks, spherical tokamaks can produce high-pressure plasmas — essential ingredients for fusion reactions — with less energy at lower costs. This shape allows for improved plasma stability, meaning it can confine high-pressure plasma more effectively for a given magnet strength, similar to getting the same horsepower from a smaller, more efficient engine. #fusion #spherical #tokamak
Jack Berkery, principal research physicist at the U.S. Department of Energy’s Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, explains how the sophisticated features of spherical tokamaks, like the National Spherical Torus Experiment-Upgrade (NSTX-U) at PPPL, enable scientists to test the viability of this compact design to reliably generate cost-effective electricity from fusion energy.
PPPL is a DOE national laboratory, managed by Princeton University. Learn more about NSTX-U: https://www.pppl.gov/nstx-u.

entry.title: We Are the Lab - Kajal Shah

media:group.media:title: We Are the Lab - Kajal Shah
media:group.media:description:
After starting her career in her home country of India, Kajal Shah knew she wanted to challenge herself to work with the best of the best, and Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory is where she knew she had to go. Her work focuses on X-ray spectroscopy, a technique that detects and measures photons, or particles of light. For fusion systems, this type of measurement helps scientists understand what’s happening inside plasma, the fuel for fusion.
Shah’s expertise supports PPPL's international collaborations with JT‑60SA, a fusion research system operated by Japan’s National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology in collaboration with Europe’s Fusion for Energy. The project is just one way that PPPL continues to amplify its impact through partnerships with companies, universities and labs across the U.S. and the world.

media:group.media:title: Why is solar shading cool?
media:group.media:description:
The Princeton Plasma Innovation Center (PPIC) is a new state-of-the-art building under construction at the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory that will support important science that advances the U.S. Department of Energy’s national priorities of AI, fusion and quantum, strengthening U.S. competitiveness.
Designed by SmithGroup and built by INTECH Construction, PPIC includes a number of features that enable it to be as efficient and high performance as possible. One of those features is passive solar shading. Across PPIC’s office wing, special fins in shades of yellow and orange line the sides of the building’s glass exterior. After hundreds of hours of careful modeling, each is arranged at a specific angle to reduce glare and heat gain, and maximize thermal comfort. The final design blocks nearly 90 percent of direct solar heat and glare, reducing cooling demand by about 30 percent, a significant energy savings.
Learn more: https://www.pppl.gov/about/our-vision/princeton-plasma-innovation-center-ppic
